slides.title: Chapter 7: Curvature
slides.notes: Open the chapter by naming the central object: a tensor field that detects whether a Riemannian manifold is locally indistinguishable from Euclidean space. Stress that curvature is built from the Levi-Civita connection, so every later identity is downstream of metric compatibility and torsion freeness. Preview the arc: build the tensor, characterize flatness, list symmetries, contract to Ricci and scalar, isolate the trace-free Weyl part, and watch what happens under conformal rescaling.

slides.title: The Riemann Curvature Endomorphism
slides.notes: Lead with the operational definition. The two double-derivatives would commute in Euclidean space, and the bracket correction is exactly what makes the expression tensorial rather than merely a second-order differential operator. Check tensoriality slot by slot: the result depends only on the pointwise values of X, Y, and Z, not on extensions. The picture of a small parallelogram with output vector R(X,Y)Z is the holonomy intuition you will return to throughout the chapter.

slides.title: Curvature as the Obstruction to Flatness
slides.notes: This is the headline theorem of the chapter. Tie the two directions together: locally Euclidean immediately gives zero curvature because Christoffel symbols vanish in the standard chart, while zero curvature lets you integrate an orthonormal parallel frame and use it to construct flat coordinates. Mention the subtle point that local flatness is genuinely a pointwise tensorial condition, and emphasize that flat tori show why global structure is not determined by local geometry.

slides.title: Algebraic Symmetries of R
slides.notes: Treat the four identities as a working checklist. The first two are direct, the pair interchange is the bookkeeping consequence, and the first Bianchi identity reflects torsion freeness. Spend a moment on dimension counting because students often suspect curvature has many more independent components than it does. Dimension two with one component motivates Gaussian curvature; dimension four with twenty components prepares the later Weyl-Ricci split.

slides.title: Sectional Curvature K(sigma)
slides.notes: Frame sectional curvature as the geometric reading of R. Independence of basis is worth verifying once, then trust it. The key fact is that knowing K on every 2-plane recovers R, so any theorem about curvature can in principle be tested by checking sectional curvatures. Connect the constant curvature values back to the model manifolds students have already met: Euclidean space, the round sphere, and hyperbolic space.

slides.title: Second Bianchi and the Ricci Identities
slides.notes: Second Bianchi is the differential analogue of the algebraic Bianchi identity and is the engine behind divergence formulas like the contracted Bianchi identity used to derive the Einstein tensor. The Ricci identity is the same statement read as a calculational rule: whenever you commute two covariant derivatives on any tensor, R appears. Note that proofs in later chapters often start with this single move.

slides.title: Contractions: Ricci and Scalar Curvature
slides.notes: Walk through the two contraction steps as a visible compression of information. The Ricci tensor is symmetric because of the pair interchange identity, and it carries the average sectional curvature in directions tangent to a given vector. Scalar curvature is the further metric trace. The contracted Bianchi identity is the technically important consequence: it forces the Einstein tensor Ric - (1/2) S g to be divergence free, which is why general relativity uses it on the left-hand side of Einstein's equation.

slides.title: The Weyl Tensor: Conformally Invariant Curvature
slides.notes: Present the Weyl tensor as what remains of R after all traces are removed. In dimensions four and higher, vanishing Weyl is the precise local condition for the metric to be conformally flat, while in dimension three Weyl vanishes automatically and a different tensor takes over. Stress orthogonality of the three pieces under the natural inner product on curvature-type tensors: this is what justifies calling W the trace-free part.

slides.title: How Curvature Transforms Under Conformal Change
slides.notes: This is the calculational climax of the chapter. Emphasize the pattern: only second-order derivatives of the conformal factor appear, and they enter as a Kulkarni-Nomizu product with g. The transformation formula for Ricci is the working tool for the Yamabe problem and prescribed scalar curvature problems. Always reconcile with the invariance of W: every term added under conformal change must live in the scalar plus trace-free Ricci subspace.

slides.title: What Chapter 7 Supplies Going Forward
slides.notes: Close by mapping each piece of the chapter to the role it will play later. Sectional curvature drives comparison theorems and Jacobi field analysis. Ricci curvature appears in volume comparison and in Einstein's equations. Scalar curvature is the variable in the Yamabe problem. Weyl is the conformally invariant residue. Encourage students to read every later curvature hypothesis as a statement about one of these pieces and to ask which Bianchi identity is doing the work behind the scenes.
